Senses.Explanation: The eye of heaven and earth is a public case phrase asked directly of Jiufeng Daoqian and raised in Zhaozhou's claim to hold that eye fast without leaking the slightest thread. An unnamed questioner asks Jiufeng what the eye is. Jiufeng first places heaven and earth within it, then answers that this itself is the eye, and says its illumination does not borrow the power of sun, moon, or stars. Later collections repeatedly reopen each turn rather than paraphrase the answer away. Zhaozhou's separate formula says he holds fast the eye of heaven and earth without leaking the slightest amount and demands that the audience understand. Wansong Xingxiu tests whether this has truly been settled and warns that even a penetrating answer can remain inside Zhaozhou's enclosure.

Senses.Explanation: A dry shit-stick is the latrine wiping-tool named by the compound. Linji Yixuan asks what dry shit-stick the person of no rank is; Deshan Xuanjian predicates it of old Shakyamuni; and Yunmen Wenyan asks what dry shit-stick an assembly seeks to chew. In Yunmen’s famous case it answers ‘What is Buddha?’ Wumen Huikai preserves Yunmen as the answerer, Dahui Zonggao repeats the case in verse, and Zhongfeng Mingben places it beside the courtyard cypress and three catties of hemp as sayings with no route for explanatory boring. Wanpu Zhao later asks Miyun Yuanwu what it is and receives only ‘Look on the field ridge.’ The records deploy the named wiping-tool in questions, predicates, answers, case titles, and commentary; they assign it no further stable gloss, and neither does this entry.

Senses.Explanation: Baizhang’s wild fox names the canonical causality case and the fox-body at the center of its retelling. In the received account an old man says that his answer 'does not fall under cause and effect' led to five hundred lives as a wild fox. Baizhang answers the repeated question 'is not blind to cause and effect'; the old man reports release and asks for a monastic funeral. Guishan later responds to the raised story by shaking a door panel, and two monks dispute the easy fall-and-release opposition. Later masters repeatedly reopen the named case: Daxin raises it in the chamber, Wansong heads it as the eighth case, Foyan Qingyuan is tested on it, Shita Xuanmi Li comments on it in a hall address, Hongfu Ziwen versifies it, and Yunju Shuai'an Fancong gives another verse. A fox narrative thus becomes a stable public-case label; the entry reports its documentary parts and later testing without adjudicating cause and effect.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records make the top of a hundred-foot pole the place where gaining entry is still insufficient and a further step is demanded, questioned, or refused. Changsha Jingcen’s verse says that even one who has gained entry is not yet genuine and must step forward from the pole-top, with the ten directions as the whole body. Wumen transmits Shishuang’s question asking how to advance, and Fojian Huiqin comments on the moment of advancement. An unnamed monastic puts the fixed question to Fadeng, while Yanguan Qi’an counters by asking what use advancement would have. These divergent responses preserve the pole-top as a public challenge rather than a fixed ladder stage.

Senses.Explanation: Step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole is the demand to move when the climb has already reached its apparent endpoint. Masters ask for the line, say some people cannot make the step, or place it beside turning beyond the moonlit curtain. Yuanwu Keqin joins it to reaching down from a sheer cliff while host and guest exchange. Other speakers warn that stopping at the pole-top still leaves no way out, while successful advance opens movement through the ten directions.

Senses.Explanation: Zhong Kui is the legendary demon-queller, attested 70 times in 43 texts. Chan records do not retell a complete outside biography; they put his name and familiar attributes to work in public answers, festival speech, verse, and appraisal. Asked for “the host within the guest,” Wuzu Fayan answers, “Zhong Kui's little sister” (鍾馗小妹). At the Double-Fifth festival, after a student says that a little ghost might display a trick, Wuzu Fayan replies, “Zhong Kui will frighten you” (鍾馗嚇你), then speaks of a protective talisman. Xiaoyin Xin makes the demon-queller dance eighteen beats (鍾馗解舞十八拍); Panshan Dabo Qian pictures him on a wall beside swords hanging in space (壁上畵鍾馗，空中懸劍戟); and Fushan Fayuan says at New Year that no strange thing is presently before them, so there is no need to paste up Zhong Kui (目前無異怪，不用貼鍾馗). His name can also be an unglossed answer: asked how to discuss words with no trace, Dongshan Shouchu says, “Zhong Kui does not read books” (鍾馗不讀書). The Zen-specific bend is this repeated use of the demon-catching figure, his household, dance, painted image, and protective posting as encounter answers and teaching-seat language; no further symbolic meaning is assigned.
